body.hook: Every year, millions of people get sick from food that looked and smelled fine. Most of those illnesses come from simple mistakes: unwashed hands, a dirty cutting board, food left out too long. Professional kitchens follow strict rules, and today so will you.

study.title: Kitchen Safety Check
study.question: How do professional kitchens keep food and people safe?
study.passage:
Kitchen rules (summary written for this lesson, based on standard food-safety guidance):
Clean: Wash hands with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds before cooking, after touching raw meat or eggs, and after using the washroom or touching your face or phone. Wash and sanitize counters and boards.
Separate: Use one cutting board for raw meat and another for ready-to-eat foods such as fruit. Never put cooked food on a plate that held raw meat.
Cook: Cook food to a safe internal temperature (for example, chicken to 74 °C), checked with a food thermometer.
Chill: Keep cold food at 4 °C or colder. Do not leave food in the danger zone (4 °C to 60 °C) for more than 2 hours.
Kitchen safety: Tie back long hair, wear an apron, turn pot handles inward, use oven mitts, carry knives point down beside your leg, and wipe up spills right away.
Station task: At five stations, find the hazard in each photo or set-up and write the rule that fixes it.
study.source: Summary written for this lesson from standard food-safety guidance (clean, separate, cook, chill).

study.title: Measure Like a Chef
study.question: Why does accurate measuring matter in cooking?
study.passage:
Measuring guide (written for this lesson):
Common metric measures: 1 cup = 250 mL, ½ cup = 125 mL, ¼ cup = 60 mL, 1 tablespoon (tbsp) = 15 mL, 1 teaspoon (tsp) = 5 mL.
Dry ingredients (flour, sugar, oats): Spoon into a dry measure until heaped, then level with the back of a knife. Don't pack flour or shake the cup. Brown sugar is the exception: pack it firmly.
Liquid ingredients (milk, oil, water): Use a clear liquid measure on the counter. Bend down so your eyes are level with the line.
Small amounts (baking soda, salt): Use measuring spoons, level them off.
Station test: Measure 1 cup of flour three ways (scooped and packed, spooned and levelled, shaken). Weigh each on a kitchen scale. A correct cup of all-purpose flour is about 130 g. Which method was closest?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; standard Canadian kitchen measures.

body.hook: A healthy snack has to do three jobs at once: taste good, keep you full until dinner and be safe to eat. Today your team designs, prepares and presents one, and a panel of classmates will judge it against your criteria.

vocabulary.definition: How the body uses food for energy, growth and health.

A grain food that keeps all parts of the grain, such as oats or whole wheat.

French for "everything in its place": getting all ingredients and tools ready before cooking.

study.title: Snack Lab
study.question: How do I design and prepare a healthy snack that meets the criteria?
study.passage:
Challenge brief (written for this lesson):
Design and prepare a healthy after-school snack for Grade 7 students. Criteria: it includes at least two of the three food-guide groups (vegetables and fruits, whole grains, protein foods); it takes no more than 25 minutes to prepare; it costs under 15 dirhams for four servings; it is safe for someone with a nut allergy; it is served attractively.
Suggested recipes: yogurt parfait with oats and berries; hummus with vegetable sticks and whole-wheat pita; whole-grain wrap with egg and spinach; fruit kebabs with a yogurt dip.
Steps: choose a recipe and check it against the criteria; set up mise en place; wash hands and sanitize the station; prepare the snack; plate four servings; clean up; present to the tasting panel.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; food-guide summary based on Canada's food guide (2019).
